column4: The branded man's portrait continues with hindering good, aggression, and sin; these are further lived traits that the bodily mark of 68:16 makes publicly identifiable.
The portrait adds harshness and the disputed epithet zanīm immediately before the motive and response that lead to branding; this ayah contributes the bearer's already distinguishing moral identity.
His possession of wealth and sons supplies the worldly status surrounding his rejection of the verses; the eventual brand overturns the identity he drew from those possessions.
After the ruin, the road, and the discerning readers, the passage explicitly calls the scene a sign for believers; it confirms that the physical remainder is meant to be read.
The overthrow of Lot's towns and the rain of baked-clay stones supplies both the ruined scene and the objects that 11:83 calls marked at the Lord.
This ayah identifies the objects in 51:34 as stones of clay sent against a criminal people, so the following divine mark is an assignment of a particular instrument to particular owners of guilt.
The punishment descending on Lot's town for transgression creates the material remainder that 29:35 says God left as a clear sign.

بَقِيَّتُ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌۭ لَّكُمْ makes what God leaves or preserves “better” for the hearers, closely joining the section's definition of أثر as a بقية to its contrast between the better remainder and preferred gain.
The ark contains a remnant left by the houses of Moses and Aaron and is itself a sign of rightful kingship; surviving objects identify a divinely appointed owner and relation.
After the destroyed people, the question asks whether any remnant of them can be seen; total erasure supplies the boundary case for the section's أثر as what remains visible after its owner is gone.
Pharaoh's body is preserved so that he may be a sign for those after him; the dead bearer becomes a surviving, readable mark of the allegiance and judgment that claimed him.
Everything perishes except God's face, and judgment and return belong to Him; permanence and dominion meet in the Lord-owner after all created marks disappear.
Worldly life is likened to vegetation that impresses, yellows, and becomes debris before the lasting outcomes arrive; it shows the chosen world's visible trace passing away.
The worldly life is only temporary enjoyment whereas the Hereafter is the enduring abode, restating the precise duration test by which the section judges preference.
The later life is declared better for the Prophet than the first, a concise reversal of preferring the nearer or earlier portion merely because it is present.
The person who fears standing before his Lord and restrains desire is the opposing character to the one who preferred worldly life in 79:38.
Paradise becomes the home of that restrained person, completing the alternative to the fire-home attached to worldly preference.
Transgression identifies the person whose preference is stated in 79:38; it contributes the moral character that the following choice and fire outcome disclose.
Coming to the Lord as a believer with righteous deeds yields the highest ranks, supplying the personal alternative to the criminal who bears the neither-dead-nor-alive fire fate in 20:74.
Everlasting gardens are the purified believers' reward, completing the opposite enduring destination after the magicians refuse to prefer Pharaoh.
The Prophet is pictured following after the rejecters' traces and nearly consuming himself in grief; the departing people leave a relational and emotional أثر even when absent.

Ships at sea are likened to aʿlām, towering visible landmarks; if that noun is heard through the section's ʿ-l-m sense of a distinguishing sign, it supplies a large-scale mark recognizable at a distance.
The raised ships are again compared to aʿlām; the lexical bridge may mean mountains rather than signs here, but either reading makes them conspicuous forms that distinguish the horizon.

Calling on Allah or the Merciful is directed toward the same bearer of the beautiful names, while the prayer voice is disciplined; it protects divine naming from both false division and improper utterance.
The question whether anyone is known as the Lord's namesake or equal makes His name uniquely distinguishing, supporting the section's demand that the owner's mark remain unmixed.
Allah alone is God and owns the beautiful names; true naming therefore identifies the one owner rather than creating competing sacred claimants.
ذَٰلِكُمُ ٱللَّهُ رَبُّكُمْ لَهُ ٱلْمُلْكُ explicitly joins “your Lord” to possession of dominion, confirming the section's owner-sense of rabb.
ذَٰلِكُمُ ٱللَّهُ رَبُّكُمْ لَهُ ٱلْمُلْكُ repeats the Lord-and-ownership formula while denying the alleged partners any possession at all.
Faces are turned about in the Fire while their bearers wish they had obeyed God and the Messenger; rejected allegiance becomes a fiery mark on the face.
The rejecter is threatened with seizure by the forelock, placing judgment on a conspicuous part of the head as the brand in 68:16 is placed on the snout.
The forelock is itself called lying and sinful, attaching moral identity to a body part in the same way a brand makes the bearer's character legible.
Radiant faces on the Day begin a direct facial distinction between good and evil outcomes, the eschatological form of reading a person's trace in the face.
Those radiant faces look toward their Lord, identifying the allegiance and hope expressed by their visible condition.
Other faces are gloomy, furnishing the contrary visible mark on the bearers of a feared outcome.
The gloomy faces expect a crushing calamity, explaining the judgment their appearance already discloses.
Faces are humbled on the overwhelming Day, making abasement bodily visible before their labor and fire destination are stated.
Those humbled faces enter a scorching fire, joining the readable facial condition to the section's alternative fire-sign.
Other faces are joyful, supplying the positive facial mark opposite the humbled, fire-bound group.
The face of one given news of a daughter darkens while he suppresses grief; an inward valuation becomes immediately readable on the face.
The same face-darkening at the news of a daughter is repeated while the man chokes with grief, confirming the face as the outward trace of a hidden preference.
God seals the disbelievers' hearts and hearing and places a covering on sight; rejection becomes an identifying divine impression upon the faculties that sustained it.
Corruption appears on land and sea because of what people's hands earned; collective choice leaves a visible environmental trace whose makers can be inferred from it.
People allocate crops and livestock between God and their alleged partners, staging rival claims of ownership that the section's true Lord-mark is meant to distinguish.
The invented livestock rules assign what is in animal wombs by sex and status; false ownership-signs continue by deciding who may possess or consume the marked stock.
Neither sacrificial flesh nor blood reaches God; piety does. This sets the boundary between an outward animal sign and the inward allegiance that gives the rite its true mark.
Hūd calls the alleged deities mere names coined by the people and their fathers without authority, exposing labels that claim sacred identity but bear no true owner's warrant.
After people fabricate sons and daughters for God, He is glorified above their descriptions; this is an explicit purification of the Lord's identity from defective attribution.
God's name is remembered in houses He allowed to be raised, so a visible place and the recurring name together identify a space as belonging to His worship.
Protected houses of worship are defined as places where God's name is mentioned often; their preservation keeps the owner's name visibly present in the world.
Worldly life is play and distraction while the Hereafter is the true life, sharpening the section's claim that preference reveals whether one bears a passing or lasting attachment.
Worldly embellishment is called mere enjoyment, while the Hereafter with the Lord belongs to the mindful; the owner and the enduring destination determine the better preference.
The wind destroys the people so completely that only their dwellings can be seen; ownerless structures remain as readable traces of vanished bearers and judgment.
The wrongdoers' houses lie empty because of what they did, and the scene is called a sign for those who know; ruin functions as an identifying remainder.
Ruined towns, collapsed roofs, abandoned wells, and lofty palaces present the surviving objects of destroyed communities, concrete آثار from which their fate is read.
